words.definition: Moderate or restrained, especially in eating and drinking.
words.example: Despite the lavish buffet, she remained abstemious, taking only a small salad.
words.mnemonic: Contains all five vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in order — disciplined, just like the word's meaning.

words.definition: Given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behavior.
words.example: The capricious manager fired employees one day and praised them the next.
words.mnemonic: Think Capri-cious → like a goat on a Capri cliff, leaping unpredictably from ledge to ledge.

words.definition: To criticize unfairly; to attack the reputation of.
words.example: Critics denigrated the novel before it even reached bookstores.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'nigr' (black) — to blacken someone's name.

words.definition: Cheerful and full of energy; overflowing with enthusiasm.
words.example: Her ebullient personality made even dull meetings feel celebratory.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'boiling' — picture feelings boiling over with joy.

words.definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; hard to please.
words.example: He was fastidious about grammar, correcting every stray comma.
words.mnemonic: 'Fast' + 'tedious' — a fast person fussing tediously over every detail.

words.definition: Excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters.
words.example: Our garrulous uncle can turn a simple greeting into a forty-minute monologue.
words.mnemonic: 'Gargle' + 'loose' — mouth gargles with loose, endless chatter.

words.definition: Overused to the point of being unoriginal and stale.
words.example: 'Love conquers all' is a hackneyed phrase that has lost its punch.
words.mnemonic: A 'hackney' was an overworked carriage horse — ideas ridden to exhaustion.

words.definition: A person who attacks cherished beliefs, traditions, or institutions.
words.example: Galileo was an iconoclast whose ideas overturned centuries of dogma.
words.mnemonic: 'Icon' (image) + 'clast' (break) — one who breaks sacred images.

words.definition: Naive, simplistic, and superficial; lacking substance.
words.example: His jejune analysis of the war ignored the economic forces behind it.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'June' — the month school ends and jejune minds wander.

words.definition: To act in an excessively subservient manner; to grovel.
words.example: She refused to kowtow to a boss who demanded flattery.
words.mnemonic: From Chinese 'ke tou' — to knock one's head on the ground in submission.

words.definition: Using very few words; terse.
words.example: His laconic reply — 'fine' — gave away none of his feelings.
words.mnemonic: The Laconians (Spartans) were famous for short, blunt speech.

words.definition: Not truthful; habitually lying.
words.example: The mendacious salesman promised features the product didn't have.
words.mnemonic: Think 'men-dacious' — men who make fibs tell 'mendacious' tales.

words.definition: The lowest point of something; the point of greatest adversity.
words.example: Losing her job and her home marked the nadir of her year.
words.mnemonic: From Arabic 'nazir' (opposite) — opposite of zenith, the highest point.

words.definition: Obedient or attentive to an excessive, servile degree.
words.example: The obsequious waiter nodded at every word, praising our every choice.
words.mnemonic: 'Ob-' (toward) + 'sequi' (follow) — follows too eagerly, to the point of fawning.

words.definition: Transparently clear in style or meaning; easy to understand.
words.example: Her pellucid explanation made quantum physics seem almost simple.
words.mnemonic: 'Pel-' (through) + 'lucid' (light) — light passes through.

words.definition: Exceedingly idealistic; unrealistic and impractical.
words.example: His quixotic plan to end poverty with a single app drew gentle smiles.
words.mnemonic: From Don Quixote, the knight who tilted at windmills thinking they were giants.

words.definition: Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority.
words.example: The recalcitrant student refused every attempt to engage him.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (back) + 'calcitr' (kick) — kicks back against every instruction.

words.definition: Health-giving; promoting well-being.
words.example: They moved to the coast for the salubrious sea air.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'salute your health' — a salubrious toast.

words.definition: Reserved or uncommunicative in speech; saying little.
words.example: Her taciturn neighbor had lived next door for years without a real conversation.
words.mnemonic: 'Tacit' (silent) + '-urn' — silent as an urn.

words.definition: Present, appearing, or found everywhere.
words.example: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern life.
words.mnemonic: Think 'U-be-quick-to-us' — it's already everywhere before you notice.

words.definition: To alternate or waver between different opinions or actions.
words.example: He vacillated for weeks before finally accepting the offer.
words.mnemonic: Think 'vacation late' — can't decide when to leave, keeps swaying.

words.definition: Deliberate, unprovoked, and without motive; reckless.
words.example: The wanton destruction of the park shocked the entire neighborhood.
words.mnemonic: 'Want-on' — wanting on with harm, without reason or limit.

words.definition: Dislike of or prejudice against people from other countries.
words.example: The rise in xenophobia made immigrants fear for their safety.
words.mnemonic: 'Xeno' (foreign) + 'phobia' (fear) — fear of foreigners.

words.definition: A burden or oppressive force; also, to join together.
words.example: They finally threw off the yoke of colonial rule.
words.mnemonic: Picture oxen yoked together — bound by a heavy wooden frame.

words.definition: A person who is fanatically devoted to a cause.
words.example: The reformer was seen as a zealot by those who preferred the status quo.
words.mnemonic: 'Zeal' + '-ot' — someone whose zeal is dialed up to the max.

words.definition: Something that belongs to a different time period than the one depicted.
words.example: A wristwatch in a Roman epic is a glaring anachronism.
words.mnemonic: 'Ana-' (against) + 'chronos' (time) — against its time.

words.definition: High-sounding but with little meaning; inflated language.
words.example: His bombastic speech used grand words to say almost nothing.
words.mnemonic: Like a 'bomb' of hot air — loud, empty, and inflated.

words.definition: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds.
words.example: The orchestra's warm-up was a cacophony of tuning strings and horns.
words.mnemonic: 'Caco-' (bad) + 'phony' (sound) — bad sounds.

words.definition: Light, delicate, and translucent.
words.example: Her diaphanous veil floated like mist in the breeze.
words.mnemonic: 'Dia-' (through) + 'phan' (show) — light shows through.

words.definition: Bubbly and lively; giving off bubbles.
words.example: Her effervescent laugh lit up the entire dinner party.
words.mnemonic: Picture fizzy water — always bubbling with cheer.

words.definition: Excessively elaborate or ornate; reddish in complexion.
words.example: The critic mocked the novel's florid prose and purple descriptions.
words.mnemonic: 'Flora' (flowers) — flowery writing, overflowing with ornament.

words.definition: Fond of the company of others; sociable.
words.example: Gregarious by nature, he knew every neighbor on the block.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'grex' (flock) — happiest among the flock.

words.definition: Denoting a period of time that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
words.example: She reminisced about the halcyon days of her childhood summers.
words.mnemonic: Greek myth: a bird calmed the seas — halcyon days are calm days.

words.definition: Unable to be upset or excited; calm.
words.example: Even in chaos, the surgeon remained imperturbable.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-' (not) + 'perturbable' (disturbed) — not disturbed.

words.definition: To place close together for contrasting effect.
words.example: The exhibit juxtaposes Renaissance and modern portraits.
words.mnemonic: 'Juxta' (next to) + 'pose' (place) — place next to each other.

words.definition: The sound of a bell, especially a funeral bell; a sign of the end.
words.example: The closing factory sounded the knell of the town's prosperity.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'bell' — a somber, final bell.

words.definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal.
words.example: His lugubrious expression suggested something had gone very wrong.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'loo-goo-brious' — a mournful, drawn-out groan.

words.definition: To pretend illness to escape duty or work.
words.example: He malingered for a week to skip the big deadline.
words.mnemonic: 'Mal-' (bad) + 'linger' — lingering in bed under false pretenses.

words.definition: Vague, hazy, or ill-defined.
words.example: His plans for the business were nebulous at best.
words.mnemonic: 'Nebula' — a cloudy, indistinct cluster of gas.

words.definition: To deliberately make something unclear or hard to understand.
words.example: The lawyer obfuscated the timeline with irrelevant details.
words.mnemonic: 'Ob-' (over) + 'fuscate' (darken) — cast darkness over the truth.

words.definition: A solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases.
words.example: There is no panacea for a troubled economy.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'pan' (all) + 'akos' (cure) — cure for all.

words.definition: Of or occurring every day; daily and ordinary.
words.example: She found beauty in the quotidian routines of cooking and cleaning.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'quotidie' (every day) — the daily grind.

words.definition: Little known; obscure; dealing with abstruse subjects.
words.example: His lecture on recondite medieval logic lost half the audience.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' + 'condite' (hidden) — knowledge hidden away, hard to find.

words.definition: A person who acts obsequiously toward someone important to gain advantage.
words.example: The CEO was surrounded by sycophants who laughed at every joke.
words.mnemonic: Think 'psycho-fan' — a pathologically fawning follower.

words.definition: Eager or quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.
words.example: His truculent tone made negotiation impossible.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'truck-you-lent' — picture a belligerent trucker spoiling for a fight.

words.definition: Offense or annoyance.
words.example: She took umbrage at the suggestion that she had been careless.
words.mnemonic: From 'umbra' (shadow) — a shadow cast over someone's feelings.

words.definition: To regard with great respect; to revere.
words.example: Students venerated the old professor for her decades of scholarship.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'Venus' — treat as holy, like the goddess of love.

words.definition: Charming, attractive, or appealing in a fresh, innocent way.
words.example: Her winsome smile disarmed even the grumpiest customers.
words.mnemonic: 'Win' + 'some' — wins some hearts with simple charm.

words.definition: The highest point or state; the peak.
words.example: Winning the championship marked the zenith of her career.
words.mnemonic: Opposite of nadir — zenith is up in the zed (sky).

words.definition: Sharp and forthright in speech or manner; biting.
words.example: His acerbic wit left no target untouched.
words.mnemonic: Think 'acid' — acerbic words have an acid bite.

words.definition: Demonstrating aggression and willingness to fight.
words.example: The bellicose speech only made the crisis worse.
words.mnemonic: 'Belli-' (war, as in 'rebellion') — warlike in temper.

words.definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
words.example: She offered a cogent argument that swayed the entire committee.
words.mnemonic: 'Co-' + 'gent' — ideas act together, forcing agreement.

words.definition: Slow to act; intended to cause delay.
words.example: His dilatory tactics pushed the trial back by months.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'delay' — dilatory equals delayed.

words.definition: Lasting for a very short time.
words.example: Fame on social media can be strikingly ephemeral.
words.mnemonic: 'Epi-' (on) + 'hemera' (day) — lasts only a day.

words.definition: Producing or capable of producing an abundance; fruitful.
words.example: The artist had a fecund imagination that never seemed to tire.
words.mnemonic: Think 'fruit-cund' — fruitful and abundant.

words.definition: Pompous or extravagant in language or style.
words.example: His grandiloquent toast embarrassed the modest bride.
words.mnemonic: 'Grand' + 'eloquent' — eloquence turned up too grand.

words.definition: Overly theatrical or melodramatic.
words.example: Her histrionic reaction to the minor delay startled everyone.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'histrio' (actor) — acting like you're on stage.

words.definition: Having little or no money.
words.example: The impecunious student survived on ramen and hope.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-' (not) + 'pecunia' (money) — no money.

words.definition: Extreme patriotism, especially in the form of aggressive foreign policy.
words.example: The editorial warned against the rise of jingoism in political rhetoric.
words.mnemonic: From an old British war song with the line 'by jingo!' — chauvinist cheering.

words.definition: Relating to or resulting from motion.
words.example: The dancer had a kinetic energy that electrified the stage.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'cinema' — motion pictures.

words.definition: A state of physical or mental weariness; lack of energy.
words.example: A deep lassitude followed the long week of exams.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'lazy' — lassitude = heavy laziness.

words.definition: Self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental.
words.example: After two glasses of wine he grew maudlin about his college days.
words.mnemonic: From Mary Magdalene, often depicted weeping in art.

words.definition: Just coming into existence; beginning to develop.
words.example: The nascent startup had only three employees and one prototype.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'natal' — newly born.

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action.
words.example: He remained obdurate despite every plea from his family.
words.mnemonic: 'Ob-' + 'durate' (hardened) — hardened against persuasion.

words.definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual way.
words.example: The pernicious influence of misinformation spreads slowly but widely.
words.mnemonic: 'Per-' (through) + 'nic-' (harm) — harmful through and through.

words.definition: Complaining in a petulant or whining manner.
words.example: The querulous toddler objected to every meal.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'quarrel' — always picking at something.

words.definition: The tendency of a convicted criminal to reoffend.
words.example: The program reduced recidivism by offering job training.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + 'cid' (fall) — falling back into crime.

words.definition: Optimistic or positive, especially in a difficult situation.
words.example: She remained sanguine about the project despite repeated setbacks.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'sanguis' (blood) — the old humor of cheerful blood.

words.definition: Very weak or slight; flimsy.
words.example: The evidence connecting the two events was tenuous at best.
words.mnemonic: Think 'thin-yous' — stretched thin.

words.definition: The condition of being in a definite place; 'whereness.'
words.example: The philosopher pondered the ubiety of consciousness itself.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ubi' (where) — the state of being somewhere.

words.definition: The appearance of being true or real.
words.example: The novel's verisimilitude made the fictional city feel genuine.
words.mnemonic: 'Veri' (true) + 'similis' (similar) — similar to the truth.

words.definition: A large number of items in no order; a confused mass.
words.example: A welter of receipts spilled out of the shoebox.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'swelter' — a hot, jumbled mess.

words.definition: An animal, especially a calf, sheep, or horse, one year old.
words.example: The trainer evaluated each yearling for racing potential.
words.mnemonic: 'Year' + '-ling' — a young thing one year old.

words.definition: A departure from what is normal, usual, or expected.
words.example: His rudeness was an aberration; he's usually quite polite.
words.mnemonic: 'Ab-' (away) + 'err' (stray) — a straying away.

words.definition: To charm, often in a deceptive way; to pass time pleasantly.
words.example: The salesman beguiled them into signing the contract.
words.mnemonic: 'Be-' + 'guile' (deception) — use guile to charm.

words.definition: To reprimand someone severely.
words.example: The coach castigated the team for their sloppy performance.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'chastise' — a stern scolding.

words.definition: A scarcity or lack of something.
words.example: There was a dearth of qualified candidates for the position.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'death' of supply — extreme scarcity.

words.definition: Mental calmness and composure, especially under stress.
words.example: She accepted the criticism with equanimity and moved on.
words.mnemonic: 'Equi' (equal) + 'animus' (mind) — mind in balance.

words.definition: Silly and pointless; foolishly self-satisfied.
words.example: His fatuous grin suggested he hadn't understood the question.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fat-you-us' — a foolishly complacent puffed-up remark.

words.definition: Relevant to a subject under consideration.
words.example: Please keep your comments germane to the agenda.
words.mnemonic: Think 'germ' of the idea — close kin to the topic.

words.definition: A lengthy and aggressive speech; to lecture angrily.
words.example: The coach delivered a twenty-minute harangue about discipline.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'hair-rang' — voice rings loud enough to rattle your hair.

words.definition: Just begun and so not fully formed or developed.
words.example: She had an inchoate sense that something was wrong, but no proof.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-coat' — still putting its coat on, not ready.

words.definition: Cheerful and lighthearted.
words.example: The jocund crowd sang along with every song.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'jocular' — full of jokes and good humor.

words.definition: Tearful or given to weeping; mournful.
words.example: The lachrymose film had the entire theater reaching for tissues.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'lacrima' (tear) — full of tears.

words.definition: Pleasingly smooth and musical to hear.
words.example: Her mellifluous voice made every bedtime story magical.
words.mnemonic: 'Mel' (honey) + 'fluere' (flow) — honey flowing from the tongue.

words.definition: Wicked, villainous, or criminal.
words.example: The spy's nefarious plan almost succeeded.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ne-furious' — furiously evil.

words.definition: Harsh criticism or public disgrace.
words.example: The scandal brought opprobrium on the entire administration.
words.mnemonic: 'Op-' (against) + 'probrum' (disgrace) — heaped disgrace.

words.definition: Extremely poor; stingy with money.
words.example: Their penurious landlord refused to fix even the broken window.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'penury' — severe poverty.

words.definition: In a state of inactivity or dormancy.
words.example: The volcano had been quiescent for two centuries.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'quiet' — resting silently.

words.definition: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved.
words.example: He was reticent about his past, deflecting every personal question.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' + 'tacent' (silent) — keeps things silent.
